opus-5.5.text:
I think we're at a very exciting but also very early moment. Over the last two or three years, the biggest change has come from bringing large foundation models into robotics. Before that, every robot skill was trained more or less from scratch: one policy for picking, another for opening a drawer, and none of them generalized beyond the lab setup where they were trained. Now, with vision-language-action models, a robot can inherit a lot of common sense from internet-scale data. It can understand an instruction it has never seen, recognize objects it was never trained on, and do some reasoning about what to do next. That semantic generalization has improved dramatically.

Where we're still far behind is the physical side: dexterity, robustness, and reliability. A robot today might fold a shirt or pack a lunch box in a demo, but if you look at the success rate over thousands of trials, in messy, unstructured homes, it's nowhere near what you'd need for a real product. The last few percentage points of reliability are the hardest, and in the physical world mistakes are costly. You can't just regenerate the answer like a chatbot when you've broken a glass.

The other fundamental bottleneck is data. Language models had the whole internet. Robotics doesn't have an equivalent, so we rely on teleoperation, simulation, and human videos, and none of these alone is enough yet. I believe whoever figures out how to scale robot data efficiently will unlock the next big jump.

On timelines, I'd say we'll see robots doing useful work in more structured settings, like factories, warehouses, and logistics, within the next few years. That's already starting. A general-purpose robot in the home that can reliably do most chores is harder. My personal guess is somewhere around five to ten years, though progress has been surprising us in both directions. I'm optimistic, because for the first time it feels like we have a credible technical path toward general-purpose robots, rather than just hoping for one.

r001.rationale: The response calls robotics a very early moment and says current robots lack the reliability and robustness needed for real products.

r002.rationale: It says reliable general-purpose home robots are harder and estimates five to ten years, signaling that realization will take time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd describe where we are as the moment just before a steep part of the curve, but still before it.

If you look at the hardware side, the progress over the last few years has been remarkable. Humanoid platforms are becoming affordable, actuators are getting stronger and more compliant, the hands are improving, and the supply chain is maturing fast, especially in China. A few years ago a research-grade humanoid cost hundreds of thousands of dollars; now you can get something capable for a fraction of that. So the body is less and less the bottleneck.

The real gap is intelligence. Locomotion is largely solved. With reinforcement learning and sim-to-real, we can get a quadruped or a humanoid to walk, run, climb stairs, recover from pushes, and do this robustly in the real world. I'd say that's close to a mature technology now. Manipulation is a different story. Picking up arbitrary objects in a cluttered home, folding laundry, loading a dishwasher, doing a long sequence of steps without a human resetting things, that's where today's systems still fail often. Demos look great, but the success rate and generality are not at the level where you'd leave a robot alone in your house.

The reason is data. Language models had the entire internet. Robots don't have an internet of actions. Every team is collecting teleoperation data, using simulation, trying to learn from human videos, and these are all partial solutions. I think the biggest open question in the field is which of these data sources, or which combination, will scale. We've seen foundation models for robotics that show encouraging generalization, so the direction is right, but we're at maybe the GPT-2 stage, not the GPT-4 stage.

On timelines, I'd break it into layers. Robots in structured or semi-structured environments, warehouses, factories, logistics, inspection, I think we'll see real deployment at scale within the next two to three years, and in some places it's already happening. Robots doing narrow but useful tasks in homes, maybe five years. A truly general-purpose home robot that can do most of what a person would ask, I think that's further out, maybe a decade, and I'm honestly uncertain. The uncertainty is because this depends on whether the data problem gets a breakthrough. If it does, things could move much faster than anyone expects, the way language did.

So I'm optimistic, but I try to be honest about the gap between a good video and a product that works ten thousand times in a row. That reliability gap is the whole game right now.

r001.rationale: The response says demos overstate readiness: manipulation still fails often, lacks generality, and is not reliable enough to leave robots alone at home.

r002.rationale: The response puts a truly general-purpose home robot about a decade away, says the timeline is uncertain, and ties faster progress to a data breakthrough.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between robots that perform a specific task in a controlled environment and robots that can handle many different tasks in everyday life. The first category is already useful. The second still has substantial challenges.

A compelling demonstration shows that a robot can do something, but a practical product needs to do it reliably, safely, and at an acceptable cost, over and over again. That gap is easy to underestimate. In the physical world, objects move, lighting changes, and unexpected situations occur. A robot has to cope with those variations.

So I wouldn’t give a single date for when robots will be “realized.” We’ll see progress application by application, starting where the environment is more predictable and the value is clear. General-purpose robots will take longer, and the timeline remains uncertain. I’m optimistic, but I would judge progress by how consistently robots solve real problems, rather than by their most impressive demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts successful demonstrations with the reliability, safety, and cost demands of practical products, and says that gap is easy to underestimate.

r002.rationale: It says general-purpose robots will take longer, the timeline is uncertain, and progress should be expected application by application rather than by a single date.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to separate what robots can demonstrate from what they can reliably do in everyday use. We’ve made substantial progress in mobility, perception, and learning new skills. But a robot performing a task once in a controlled setting is very different from doing it thousands of times safely, at an acceptable cost, in an unfamiliar environment.

So I don’t think there’s one date when robots will suddenly be “realized.” In structured environments, robots are already useful. For more general applications, we’ll likely see adoption task by task, starting where the environment is predictable and the economic value is clear. A robot that can help with anything around the home is a much harder problem.

I’m optimistic about the direction, but cautious about precise timelines. The important question is how quickly we can turn impressive capabilities into dependable products. That requires progress in both intelligence and hardware, and a lot of testing in the real world.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes a robot’s controlled demonstration from reliable, repeated performance in everyday or unfamiliar settings, cautioning against overstating current capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says there is no single date for general realization, calls broader applications difficult, and is cautious about timelines, conveying that progress may take substantial time.
